bib.title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance. Bansal, Wu, Zhou, Fok, Nushi, Kamar, Ribeiro, Weld. CHI 2021 (arXiv:2006.14779v3).

COVERAGE: 16 of 16 pages; 96,751 of 96,751 chars (count includes my page markers). References were skimmed. I also viewed pages 8-9 as images, because Fig 4 and 5 hold results that the text does not state.

Hyphenated line breaks are rejoined in quotes.

CLAIMS

1. No tested explanation condition significantly beat confidence-only.
   number: Beer 0.89±0.05 vs 0.88±0.06, z=-1.18, p=.24; Amzbook z=1.23, p=.22; LSAT z=0.427, p=.64
   setup: Team (Conf) vs Team (Explain-Top-1); AI source on sentiment, expert source on LSAT; about 100 per condition
   quote: "Team (Conf) and Team (Explain-Top-1, AI) achieved similar performance, with the accuracy being 0.89± 0.05 vs. 0.88± 0.06 respectively; the difference was insignificant (𝑧=-1.18, 𝑝=.24). We observed the same pattern for Amzbook (𝑧=1.23, 𝑝=.22) and LSAT (𝑧=0.427, 𝑝=.64)."
   where: p7
   These are the only effect sizes given for explanations vs confidence. Explain-Top-2 vs Conf has no printed statistic.

2. Accuracy rose with explanations when the AI was right and fell when it was wrong, for a minimal net change.
   number: none
   setup: conclusion across all datasets; per-dataset evidence is Fig 4B only
   quote: "Explanations increased team performance when the system was correct, but they decreased the accuracy on examples when the system was wrong, making the net improvement minimal."
   where: p14; hedged as "often" on p3
   My Fig 4B reading, approximate and not quotable, for Conf to Top-1:
   - AI wrong: Beer .73 to .68, LSAT .47 to .42, Amzbook .65 to .70.
   - AI right: Beer and Amzbook nearly flat, LSAT .815 to .835.
   The paper prints no split numbers and no split significance tests, apart from claim 3.

3. Amzbook is a printed exception to claim 2.
   number: 5%
   setup: AI incorrect, Explain-Top-1 vs Conf
   quote: "when the AI was incorrect, explaining predictions on Amzbook via Explain-Top-1 improved the performance by 5% over showing confidence (Figure 4B), but it decreased the performance for Beer and LSAT."
   where: p9
   The authors' guess is that Amzbook AI errors were obvious, so people learned to rely on it less. They flag possible confounds (p10).

4. "Regardless of correctness": the acceptance claim carries no number and no test.
   number: none
   setup: abstract-level claim
   quote: "explanations increased the chance that humans will accept the AI's recommendation, regardless of its correctness"
   where: p1; also "explanations increased reliance on recommendations even when the AI was incorrect" (p2) and "explanations increased blind trust rather than appropriate reliance" (p12)
   Fig 5 (agreement) contains no Team (Conf) row, so agreement with vs without explanations is never shown. The evidence against the baseline is the accuracy split in Fig 4B, which is an inference about acceptance. Claim 3 also qualifies "regardless". This is my reading of the figures and text.

5. Every team condition was complementary, including confidence-only.
   number: Beer 0.89 vs AI 0.84 vs human 0.82±0.09; relative gains 2.2% (Amzbook), 20.1% (LSAT)
   setup: Team (Conf) vs baselines
   quote: "increased their performance to (𝜇 = 0.89± 𝜎 = 0.05), surpassing both AI (0.84) and unassisted human accuracy (0.82± 0.09). Similarly, Team (Conf) achieved complementary performance for Amzbook and LSAT, with relative gains of 2.2% and 20.1% over unassisted workers"
   where: p7
   No test statistic is printed for these gains.

6. Adaptive explanations did not improve accuracy.
   number: Beer z=-1.02, p=.31; Amzbook z=1.08, p=.28; LSAT z=0.16, p=.87
   setup: Adaptive vs Conf; AI source on sentiment, expert source on LSAT
   quote: "Team (Adaptive, AI) and Team (Conf) for Beer (𝑧=-1.02, 𝑝=.31) or Amzbook (𝑧=1.08, 𝑝=.28). We did not observe significant differences between Team (Adaptive, Expert) and Team (Conf) for LSAT (𝑧=0.16, 𝑝=.87)."
   where: pp7-8

7. Adaptive did shift agreement in the intended direction, shown only in a figure. Authors call this "suggestive" (p2).
   number: none in text; Fig 5 reading is roughly .77 to .71 for Beer low-confidence items (approximate)
   setup: split by adaptive threshold; explanation conditions only; LSAT intervals overlap visually
   quote: "Adaptive explanations successfully reduced the human's tendency to blindly trust the AI (i.e., decreased agreement) when it was uncertain and more likely to be incorrect."
   where: p9, Fig 5 caption
   Stated reason accuracy did not follow: people still had to catch high-confidence errors and solve low-confidence items themselves (pp8-9).

8. Expert explanations did not beat AI ones, despite being higher quality.
   number: Beer z=1.31, p=.19; Amzbook z=-0.78, p=.43
   setup: Adaptive Expert vs Adaptive AI
   quote: "the differences in performance between Team (Adaptive, Expert) and Team (Adaptive, AI) were insignificant: Beer (𝑧=1.31, 𝑝=.19) and Amzbook (𝑧=-0.78, 𝑝=.43)."
   where: p8

9. Explain-Top-1 vs Top-2: not significant.
   number: Beer z=0.85, p=.40; Amzbook z=0.81, p=.42; LSAT z=0.42, p=.68
   setup: all three tasks; H1 unsupported
   quote: "the difference was not significant (𝑧=0.85, 𝑝=.40). The same was true for Amzbook (𝑧=0.81, 𝑝=.42) and LSAT (𝑧=0.42, 𝑝=.68)."
   where: p7

10. Study design: tasks and AI accuracy.
    number: 50 examples each at 84% AI accuracy; pilot humans 87% and 85%; LSAT 20 questions, AI 65% vs human 67%
    setup: RoBERTa fine-tuned; LIME highlights (isotonic calibration) on sentiment; LSAT explanations expert-written only, because no automated method worked
    quote: "87% for Beer and 85% for Amzbook" ... "selected 50 unambiguous examples so that the AI's accuracy was 84%" (p5); "The RoBERTa model achieved 65% accuracy on these examples, comparable to the 67% human accuracy that we observed in our pilot study." (p6)
    AI accuracy was fixed by selecting examples, not by the model's general accuracy. Final-study humans differed from the pilots: Beer 0.82 printed (p7), LSAT about .58 in Fig 4A (approximate).

11. Participants and conditions.
    number: 566, 552, 508 recruited; 84%, 84%, 35% passed; 93-101 per condition
    setup: MTurk, US only, at least 97% approval, at least 1,000 approved tasks; between-subject random assignment; gated by screening; immediate feedback after each item; pay about $15.77/hr and $23.34/hr with accuracy bonuses
    quote: "we recruited 566 (Beer) and 552 (Amzbook) crowd workers, and in both datasets, 84% of participants passed the screening and post-filtering" (p7); "508 crowd workers participated in our study, 35% of whom passed the screening" (p7); "studies with 1626 users on three tasks" (p2)
    Conditions: Human; Team (Conf); Explain-Top-1; Explain-Top-2; Adaptive (threshold is median confidence, 89.2% Beer, 88.9% Amzbook, p6); Adaptive Expert. LSAT has no AI-source explanations. Every explanation condition also shows confidence (p5).

12. Definition of complementary performance.
    number: zone "( max (Human, AI) , 1 ]" (Fig 1, p2)
    setup: scored on decision accuracy only
    quote: "complementary performance, where team accuracy is higher than either the human or the AI working solo"
    where: p1

13. Earlier studies differ because the AI alone beat the team, so explanations only pulled the team toward the AI.
    number: e.g. deceptive reviews 51.1% human, 87.0% AI, 74.6% team; income 65%, 75%, 73%; hypoxemia AUC 0.66, 0.81, 0.78
    setup: Table 1, one most-comparable sample per paper
    quote: "complementary performance was not observed in any of these studies – in each case, adding the human to the loop decreased performance compared to if AI had acted alone." (p3); table values on p4
    Possible exception: Bilgic & Mooney 2005, who had no simple baseline (p3).

14. The adaptive threshold caught most errors in sentiment.
    number: 7 of 8 errors were in the low-confidence half
    setup: Beer and Amzbook study samples
    quote: "We happened to explain 18 correctly predicted and 7 incorrectly predicted examples with Explain-Top-2 for both datasets (leaving 1 incorrect and 24 correct cases with Explain-Top-1)."
    where: p6

15. Perceived usefulness rose where accuracy did not; descriptive and untested.
    number: AI assistance useful, Adaptive Expert vs Conf: 70 vs 57%, 65 vs 49%, 63 vs 45%
    setup: post-task Likert, post hoc, no significance claimed (footnote 9)
    quote: "for Beer, 70% of the participants rated AI assistance useful with Team (Adaptive, Expert) in contrast to 57% with Team (Conf). We observed a similar pattern on Amzbook (65% vs. 49%) and LSAT (63% vs. 45%)"
    where: p10

16. Self-reported strategies: most people partly used the AI, and some used confidence as a threshold.
    number: more than 70% partial use; 27% of the 90 who cited confidence used a threshold; 13% deferred when unsure
    setup: 409 coded responses, kappa 0.71
    quote: "more than 70% of the participants mentioned they would partially take AI's recommendation into consideration" (p11); "27% reported using an explicit confidence threshold" (p11); "13% participants mentioned that they would go with the AI's decision if they were on the fence" (p12)

17. Showing the answer first may anchor people; this was not tested as a variable.
    number: none
    setup: all conditions showed the AI first; LSAT placed it on a separate pane
    quote: "All of our methods used a workflow that showed the AI's prediction (and its explanation) to the human, before they attempted to solve the problem on their own."
    where: p13

18. Comparable accuracy does not guarantee complementary errors.
    number: none
    setup: Amzbook errors correlated more strongly with humans'; shown descriptively in Fig 6
    quote: "Comparable accuracy does not guarantee complementary partners."
    where: p13

LIMITS

Authors concede (p12):
- Accuracy was the only metric; speed and other benefits were not evaluated.
- "our results may not generalize to high-stakes domains with expert users such as medical diagnosis".
- User expertise was not explored.
- "we only explored two possible ways to present explanations (highlighting keywords and natural language arguments)".
- "conducted in a limited scope" (p12).

What the paper does not show (my reading):
- It does not show that explanations never help. These are non-significant results, with no equivalence test and no power analysis printed. H2 is reported as "could not reject".
- It does not compare explanations with a bare recommendation, or with explanations minus confidence. The baseline already includes calibrated confidence, and confidence's own effect is not isolated.
- It reports no agreement or acceptance rate against the confidence baseline, and no significance test on the correct/incorrect splits.
- It does not test evidence displays such as diffs, tests or recomputed numbers, confirmation of writes, or independent-first workflows. Devil's advocate, delayed display and evidence-only ideas are proposals (pp13-14).
- It does not test LLMs, chat, agents or generated rationales. Its explanations are LIME highlights and hand-written text from 2020-era classifiers on low-stakes tasks.
- It does not test persuasion directly. The closest text is a discussion suggestion that "maximally convincing" explanations may be a poor goal (p13), plus the closing call "to increase understanding rather than just to persuade" (p14).

Dated: RoBERTa/LIME-era models and 2020 crowdworkers.

Points for the target notes (facts only):
- "More than 1,500" (p14) and 1,626 are counts of recruits before screening. 566+552+508 = 1,626 is my sum. No analysed total is printed.
- The unqualified right-up, wrong-down wording matches p14, but p9 excepts Amzbook.
- "None beat confidence" matches the paper's overall statement, but printed statistics cover only some pairs (claims 1, 6).
- "Raised trust when wrong" is the authors' interpretation of accuracy splits, not a measured trust effect.

BUILDS ON (as printed):
- Lee & See 2004 (appropriate reliance)
- Ribeiro et al. 2016 (LIME)
- Liu et al. 2019 (RoBERTa)
- Yu et al. 2020 (ReClor)
- Lai & Tan 2019; Lai et al. 2020
- Zhang et al. 2020
- Buçinca et al. 2020 (proxy tasks mislead)
- Kaur et al. 2020
- Wang et al. 2019 (anchoring in XAI)
- Green & Chen 2019
- Koehler 1991 (explanation causes agreement)
- Levine 2014 (Truth-Default Theory)
- Guo et al. 2017 (calibration)
- Hendrycks & Gimpel 2017
- Horvitz & Paek 2007 (complementary computing)

CODE: none. Data repository: https://github.com/uw-hai/Complementary-Performance (p2, footnote).

FIGURES:
- Fig 4, p8: "Team performance (with average accuracy and 95% confidence interval) achieved by different explanation conditions and baselines for three datasets". Best candidate, because panel B shows the right/wrong split at once, and it is the only source for most per-condition values.
- Fig 1, p2: "Do AI explanations lead to complementary team performance?" Shows prior-work vs this-study setup and the complementary zone faster than prose.
- Fig 5, p9: "Relative agreement rates between humans and AI". Shows the adaptive shift; note there is no Conf row.
- Fig 6, p9: "The distribution of study examples as a function of average human accuracy". Shows why overlapping errors limit gains.
- Fig 2, p6: "A screenshot of the Team (Adaptive, Expert) condition for the Amzbook reviews dataset". Shows what participants actually saw.
- Fig 7, p10: usefulness ratings.
- Fig 8, p12: collaboration strategies.
- Fig 9, p12: confidence use with and without explanations.

PROBLEMS:
- No embedded instructions. Extraction is clean except figure text; Table 2's condition marks are missing (p4).
- Test mismatch: p7 says "Student's T-tests with Bonferroni correction" but reports z values.
- By my calculation, z=0.427 gives p about .67, not the printed .64.
- LSAT counts do not reconcile: 35% of 508 is about 178, against "100 participants per condition" across 4-5 conditions (p7).
- Sentiment counts: 84% of 566 is about 475, which fits 5 conditions at about 95 rather than the 6 rows in Fig 4. How the final Human row was collected is not explained.
- "details in Appendix" (p5): no appendix exists in this PDF.
- "small percentage of users (17%)" (p12) sits beside Table 3's "17 (5%)" (p11), and the denominators are unclear.
- Fig 4 and Fig 5 readings above are visual estimates and should not be cited as printed values.
